Direct3D 9 — the most common API for games of that era.
Direct3D 11 — what most modern games in WinHub use.
Shader compilation. Try this for missing or corrupted visuals.
Vertex declarations — how geometry is described to the GPU.
The D3DX helper library games use for textures, maths and effects.
Vulkan calls. This is what DXVK and VKD3D ultimately produce.
The glue between OpenGL and Windows windows.
GDI — classic 2D Windows drawing. Menus and launchers use it heavily.
Desktop Window Manager — compositing and window effects.
Bitmap block transfers, the workhorse of 2D drawing.
Colour palettes, used by older games.
DXCore — how the app enumerates graphics adapters.
Assembly shader parsing, for older shader models.
DirectSound — the usual audio API for older games.
XAudio2 — the usual audio API for modern games.
The modern Windows audio device API (WASAPI).
Multimedia — legacy sound, MIDI and timers.
The ALSA backend — one way sound leaves Wine on the Android side.
DirectShow — cutscene and video playback. Try this when intro videos hang.
Media Foundation, the modern video pipeline. Also common for cutscenes.
Enumeration of installed codecs and capture devices.
AVI playback through the MCI interface.
DirectInput — controllers and joysticks in older games.
XInput — the modern gamepad API. Try this when a controller isn\'t detected.
Raw input — mouse and keyboard straight from the device. Common in shooters.
USB HID devices, which is what most controllers are.
Mouse cursor. Worth trying for an invisible or stuck cursor.
Window creation and management. Broad, and useful for windowing problems.
The Windows message loop — every event the program receives. Very verbose.
Title bars, borders and window frames.
Windows hooks, which intercept events. Overlays and anti-cheat use these.
The standard Windows controls, as a group.
The Windows shell — folders, icons and file associations.
Process creation and exit. Good for a game that closes immediately.
DLL loading — which libraries the game pulls in. Very useful early on.
Each DLL as it loads, one line apiece. Cheap and often enough on its own.
Memory allocation. Verbose, but the place to look for memory corruption.
Locks, mutexes and synchronisation. The channel for a hang or deadlock.
The lowest-level Windows library. Broad and noisy.
Kernel-side calls, used by drivers and anti-cheat.
Environment variables as the process sees them.
Process and module enumeration, used by tools and anti-cheat.
The Microsoft C runtime — the standard library most games link against.
DOS interrupt 21h, for very old software.
File opens, reads and writes. Broad, and the channel for a missing-file problem.
Registry reads and writes. Good for a game that won\'t see its own settings.
Drive letter assignment — relevant to how WinHub maps your storage.
CAB archive extraction, used by installers.
INI file reads and writes. Older games keep settings this way.
Path handling and conversion between Windows and Linux paths.
Sockets — the base of nearly all networking. Start here for online problems.
Network adapter and IP configuration queries.
Remote procedure calls, used between Windows components.
Advanced Windows APIs: services, registry and security.
Windows Installer. The channel for a failing .msi install.
The embedded web browser control, used by some launchers.
Side-by-side assembly resolution, the same family as actctx.
Font loading and matching. The channel for missing or wrong text.
Locale and codepage handling — relevant to non-English text.
Input method editors, for CJK text entry.
The Wayland display driver, used by the experimental Wayland path.
Display modes and refresh rates under X11.
The macOS display driver. Not used on Android.
